I read the article in detail in the past and from my understanding they essentially have a photovoltaic device where the front and back contacts are operating as the anode and cathode for an electrolysis process. There is some novel work done here in the specific catalysts used in the anode and cathode, which is interesting, and there may be some leveraged surface effects at work here which are uniquely exploitable by the planar design of a photovoltaic device, but it mostly seems like they're just doing both steps simultaneously. That is to say, they are generating electrical current within the PV device which is in short circuit with the electrolyte solution, thereby generating hydrogen through electrolysis.

The modularized equivalent would be two discrete units, one generating electrical energy through a solar array and another generating hydrogen by electrolysis. If hydrogen generation were your end goal, you would strive to minimize transmission losses between the units. On short length scales, transmission losses less than 5% should be feasible, leaving you only with inefficiencies of electrolytic conversion-- which, calculated rigorously, would need to beat (10/(15.5*95))=67.9% to match this technology. It's possible that further advances might improve their margin, but there are also other problems with their design that leave me dubious.

Solar collection efficiency is greatly decreased by placing the PV device in water and then encapsulating it. The intensity of incident light will be lower for that alone. On top of that, the devices require additional infrastructure to flow water over the device, and would require manual servicing to reduce membrane fouling which will occur as part of the device's design, an overhead expense not needed for a traditional PV array.

EDIT: I also forgot-- water doesn't play very well with most semiconductor stacks. We go through quite a lot of pains to keep it out where possible, and test our devices with pressure and heat in wet environments to make sure they hold up. Intentionally sticking the device in water will cut operational lifetime by quite a lot right out of the gate.

I didn't know normal leaves generated hydrogen, so how can they compare this? I thought leaves generated oxygen as a biproduct of the generation of sugars, and then consumed that oxygen to burn the sugars, but still leaving some oxygen as a surplus (as long as there is enough sunlight)

Half right...leaves do produce oxygen; specifically in the Chloroplasts of cells - primarily 'Palisade Mesophyll' cells just below the surface of the leaf. However these oxygen molecules are only produced as a by-product of photosynthesis.

In Short: This oxygen is released by using energy from sunlight to split water molecules - when these are split you are left with said oxygen and two hydrogen molecules (H2O) which are no longer bound to it...the hydrogen is the important part as, in short, it holds the energy absorbed from the sunlight and can then be used by the chloroplasts to (indirectly) synthesise carbohydrates - which serve as long term energy storage.

Long story: The internal structure the Chloroplast organelle is full of folded (disk shaped) membranes known as Thylakoid(s). Complex protein structures known as photosystems (types I & II) sit on this membrane and contain the chemical Chlorophyll, when high energy photons from sunlight reach these proteins, they hit the chlorophyll molecules, and in doing so excite them.

In photosystem I, eventually enough energy builds up that it is able to catalyse the splitting of a water molecule; in doing this you get a single Oxygen atom (which will 'look' to react with another O, to form O2) and 2 Hydrogen atoms - however part of the reaction involves ionising these hydrogen atoms by removing each of their electrons (e-), in doing this they become hydrogen ions (H+) and are highly reactive.

The loose electrons travel through a series of integral proteins known as the 'electron transport chain', eventually they arrive at a photosystem II protein, which once again uses Chlorophyll molecules to absorb energy from incoming photons. This time however the absorbed energy is used to excite the electrons further - by this point the electrons are highly polarized and contain enough energy that two of them together are able to cause a H+ (from outside the Thylakoid) to react with a NADP+ molecule, the electrons join with the product of this reaction - NADPH...these are then used by the chloroplasts to produce the carbohydrate Glucose in what's known as the 'Calvin Cycle' - which is how plants absorb CO2.

Meanwhile the H+ ions created from photosystem I are used as an energy source to phosphorylate an ADP (adenosine DI phosphate) into an (adenosine TRI phosphate) molecule - THE ENERGY SOURCE OF JUST ABOUT EVERY CHEMICAL REACTION IN LIVING ORGANISMS.
